claim: Kv2.1 is a voltage-gated K+ channel that serves a major structural role in the soma and proximal dendrites of mammalian brain neurons.
source: The voltage-gated K+ channel Kv2.1 serves a major structural role in the soma and proximal dendrites of mammalian brain neurons, tethering the plasma membrane (PM) to endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Kv2.1 tethers the plasma membrane to the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: The voltage-gated K+ channel Kv2.1 serves a major structural role in the soma and proximal dendrites of mammalian brain neurons, tethering the plasma membrane (PM) to endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to prior work (Fox et al., 2015; Bishop et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2018; Kirmiz et al., 2018a; Kirmiz et al., 2018b).

claim: Kv2.1 clustering at neuronal ER-PM junctions is tightly regulated and highly conserved.
source: Although Kv2.1 clustering at neuronal ER-PM junctions (EPJs) is tightly regulated and highly conserved, its function remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior research cited in the introduction.

claim: Kv2.1 promotes the clustering and functional coupling of PM L-type Ca2+ channels (LTCCs) to ryanodine receptor (RyR) ER Ca2+ release channels.
source: By identifying and evaluating proteins in close spatial proximity to Kv2.1-containing EPJs, we discovered that a significant role of Kv2.1 at EPJs is to promote the clustering and functional coupling of PM L-type Ca2+ channels (LTCCs) to ryanodine receptor (RyR) ER Ca2+ release channels.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experimental approaches including imaging, proteomics, and electrophysiology throughout the manuscript.

claim: Kv2.1 clustering enhances LTCC opening at polarized membrane potentials.
source: Kv2.1 clustering also unexpectedly enhanced LTCC opening at polarized membrane potentials.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Kv2.1-LTCC-RyR triads can generate localized Ca2+ release events (Ca2+ sparks) independently of action potentials.
source: This enabled Kv2.1-LTCC-RyR triads to generate localized Ca2+ release events (i.e., Ca2+ sparks) independently of action potentials.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Kv2.1 and Kv2.2 are among the most abundant and widely expressed K+ channels in mammalian brain neurons.
source: The members of the Kv2 family of voltage-gated K+ (Kv) channels, Kv2.1 and Kv2.2, are among the most abundant and widely expressed K+ channels in mammalian brain neurons (Trimmer, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Trimmer, 2015.

claim: Kv2 channels are present in high-density clusters localized to neuronal somata, proximal dendrites, and axon initial segments.
source: Kv2 channels are present in high-density clusters localized to neuronal somata, proximal dendrites, and axon initial segments (Trimmer, 1991; Du et al., 1998; Bishop et al., 2015; Kirmiz et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: In hippocampal and cortical neurons, Kv2 channels conduct most of the delayed rectifier K+ current.
source: In hippocampal and cortical neurons, Kv2 channels conduct most of the delayed rectifier K+ current (Murakoshi and Trimmer, 1999; Du et al., 2000; Guan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Neuronal Kv2.1-mediated currents significantly influence action potential duration and repetitive firing.
source: Detailed studies have revealed the significant influence of neuronal Kv2.1-mediated currents on action potential duration and repetitive firing (e.g., Du et al., 2000; Liu and Bean, 2014; Kimm et al., 2015, etc.).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior studies.

claim: Kv2.1 clustering at EPJs is independent of K+ conductance.
source: Although Kv2.1 clustering at EPJs is tightly regulated and independent of K+ conductance (Kirmiz et al., 2018b), the physiological impact of concentrating this Kv channel at an EPJ is not known.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Kirmiz et al., 2018b.

claim: EPJs occupy approximately 10% of the PM surface area in brain neurons, predominantly within the soma and proximal dendrites.
source: In brain neurons, EPJs occupy approximately 10% of the PM surface area, predominantly within the soma and proximal dendrites (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Wu et al., 2017.

claim: The ER at many neuronal EPJs appears as a micron-diameter, flattened vesicle less than 10 nm from the PM, also called a 'subsurface cistern'.
source: By electron microscopy, the ER at many neuronal EPJs appears as a micron-diameter, flattened vesicle less than 10 nm from the PM, a structure also called a 'subsurface cistern' (Rosenbluth, 1962; Tao-Cheng, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Rosenbluth, 1962 and Tao-Cheng, 2018.

claim: Genetic variation in the CACNA1C gene encoding Cav1.2 is associated with neurodevelopmental, psychiatric and neurological disorders.
source: Their important role in brain is underscored by studies showing genetic variation in the CACNA1C gene encoding Cav1.2, the major voltage-sensing and pore forming α1 subunit expressed in brain, is associated with neurodevelopmental, psychiatric and neurological disorders (Splawski et al., 2004; Ferreira et al., 2008; Bozarth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Splawski et al., 2004; Ferreira et al., 2008; Bozarth et al., 2018.

claim: Cav1.2-containing LTCCs are clustered at specific sites on the PM where they participate in supramolecular protein complexes.
source: In both neurons and non-neuronal cells, Cav1.2-containing LTCCs are clustered at specific sites on the PM where they participate in supramolecular protein complexes that couple LTCC-mediated Ca2+ entry to specific Ca2+ signaling pathways (Dai et al., 2009; Rougier and Abriel, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Dai et al., 2009 and Rougier and Abriel, 2016.

claim: Neocortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and dentate granule cells have substantial LTCC populations in the soma and proximal dendrites.
source: Neocortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and dentate granule cells also have substantial LTCC populations in the soma and proximal dendrites (Westenbroek et al., 1990; Hell et al., 1993; Tippens et al., 2008; Berrout and Isokawa, 2009; Marshall et al., 2011; Kramer et al., 2012) representing the 'aspiny' regions (Spruston and McBain, 2007) of these neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: Somatic LTCCs uniquely contribute to transcription factor activation by mediating Ca2+ influx within specialized and compartmentalized signaling complexes.
source: Many current models of Ca2+-dependent activation of transcription factors posit that somatic LTCCs uniquely contribute to transcription factor activation by mediating Ca2+ influx within specialized and compartmentalized signaling complexes (Wheeler et al., 2008; Ma et al., 2012; Matamales, 2012; Wheeler et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2014; Cohen et al., 2015; Yap and Greenberg, 2018; Wild et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: Cav1.2-mediated Ca2+ entry is spatially and functionally coupled to ER ryanodine receptor (RyR) Ca2+ release channels at EPJs in cardiomyocytes.
source: For example, Cav1.2-mediated Ca2+ entry is spatially and functionally coupled to ER ryanodine receptor (RyR) Ca2+ release channels at EPJs constituting the cardiomyocyte junctional dyad (Shuja and Colecraft, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Shuja and Colecraft, 2018.

claim: Ca2+ sparks arise from clusters of RyRs located in the ER of EPJs and are triggered via local Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (CICR).
source: Localized Ca2+ release events (spreading <2 µm from the point of origin) called Ca2+ sparks arise from clusters of RyRs located in the ER of EPJs and are triggered via local Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (CICR), a feed-forward phenomenon in which cytosolic Ca2+ binding to RyRs triggers their opening (Cheng et al., 1993; Cheng and Lederer, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Cheng et al., 1993 and Cheng and Lederer, 2008.

claim: Localized RyR-mediated Ca2+ release events occur in the somata and proximal dendrites of cultured and acute slice preparations of hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: Localized RyR-mediated Ca2+ release events occur in the somata and proximal dendrites of cultured and acute slice preparations of hippocampal pyramidal neurons (Koizumi et al., 1999; Berrout and Isokawa, 2009; Manita and Ross, 2009; Miyazaki et al., 2012), but a specific molecular structure underlying these events has not been described.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior studies.

claim: Endogenous Cav1.2 channels are distributed to PM-localized clusters on the soma and proximal dendrites in mature CHNs, distinct from their punctate localization in more distal postsynaptic compartments.
source: In mature CHNs, endogenous Cav1.2 channels are distributed to PM-localized clusters on the soma and proximal dendrites, distinct from their punctate localization in the more distal postsynaptic compartments that also contain the scaffolding protein PSD-95 (Di Biase et al., 2008) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1A showing immunolabeling of Cav1.2 and PSD-95.

claim: Clusters of Kv2.1 are spatially associated with smaller Cav1.2 clusters but not Kv4.2 clusters in CHNs.
source: In CHNs expressing detectable levels of all three immunolabeling signals, presumed to be pyramidal neurons based on their morphological characteristics (Benson et al., 1994; Antonucci et al., 2001; Obermair et al., 2003), we observed clusters of Kv2.1 that were spatially associated with smaller Cav1.2 clusters but not Kv4.2 clusters (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1B showing triple immunolabeling.

claim: Many clusters of spatially associated Kv2.1 and Cav1.2 channels are colocalized with RyRs in CHNs.
source: Triple immunolabeling for Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyRs demonstrated that many of the clusters of spatially associated Kv2.1 and Cav1.2 channels were colocalized with RyRs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1C showing triple immunolabeling.

claim: There is greater spatial correlation between Cav1.2 and Kv2.1 immunolabeling than between Cav1.2 and Kv4.2 in CHNs.
source: Analysis of Pearson's Correlation Coefficient (PCC) of Cav1.2 and either Kv2.1 or Kv4.2 pixel intensity demonstrated a greater spatial correlation between Cav1.2 and Kv2.1 immunolabeling than that of Cav1.2 and Kv4.2 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1E showing PCC analysis.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the PCC of Kv2.1 and Cav1.2, and the PCC of Cav1.2 and RyRs within the same cell.
source: In support of a spatial association between Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyRs, we determined that there was a positive correlation between the PCC of Kv2.1 and Cav1.2, and the PCC of Cav1.2 and RyRs within the same cell (Figure 1F), suggesting that increased association between Cav1.2 and Kv2.1 was also associated with greater spatial coupling of Cav1.2 to RyRs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1F showing correlation analysis.

claim: Kv2.1 clusters often encompass smaller clusters of Cav1.2 and Cav1.3 in CHNs.
source: These images revealed that Kv2.1 clusters often encompassed smaller clusters of Cav1.2 as well Cav1.3 (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1G-H showing super-resolution imaging.

claim: The spatial distributions of somatic Kv2.1 and Cav1.2 puncta significantly correlate and cannot be recapitulated by random distribution.
source: We found that the spatial distributions of somatic Kv2.1 and Cav1.2 puncta significantly correlated (p<0.001 versus the null hypothesis that the spatial distributions of Kv2.1 and Cav1.2 puncta were independent) and could not be recapitulated in images in which their relative positions had been iteratively randomized in silico.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing nearest-neighbor distance analysis.

claim: Cav1.3 clusters are spatially associated with RyR clusters in CHNs.
source: We also observed similar expression patterns of endogenous Cav1.3 and RyRs in CHNs, with Cav1.3 clusters spatially associated with RyR clusters (Figure 1I), in agreement with a recent report (Sahu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1I, with citation to Sahu et al., 2019.

claim: Glutamate stimulation of CHNs reduces Kv2.1 clustering, decreases colocalization between Cav1.2 and RyRs, decreases the size of somatic RyR clusters, and increases the distance between somatic Cav1.2 clusters.
source: We found that glutamate stimulation of CHNs not only reduced Kv2.1 clustering, but also significantly decreased the colocalization between Cav1.2 and RyRs, decreased the size of somatic RyR clusters, and increased the distance between somatic Cav1.2 clusters (Figure 1J–N).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1J-N showing effects of glutamate treatment.

claim: Suppression of neuronal activity with TTX increases spatial coupling between RyRs and Cav1.2, and increases the size of individual RyR clusters.
source: Conversely, suppression of neuronal excitability with TTX produced an effect opposite of glutamate treatment, producing increased spatial coupling between RyRs and Cav1.2, and increasing the size of individual RyR clusters (Figure 1J–N).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1J-N showing effects of TTX treatment.

claim: Glutamate stimulation reduces the number of Cav1.2 clusters present on the PM.
source: We also found that glutamate stimulation reduced the number of Cav1.2 clusters present on the PM, consistent with previous observations that acute Ca2+ influx results in endocytosis of Cav1.2 channels (Hall et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Hall et al., 2013.

claim: In hippocampal neurons, Cav1.2 localizes to distinct clusters on somata and proximal dendrites, similar to Kv2.1.
source: Previous immunohistochemical analyses showed that in hippocampal neurons, Cav1.2 localizes to distinct clusters on somata and proximal dendrites (Westenbroek et al., 1990; Hell et al., 1993), a spatial pattern similar to that of Kv2.1 (Trimmer, 1991; Scannevin et al., 1996; Kirizs et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior studies.

claim: Cav1.2 immunolabeling is concentrated in CA1 neuron somata, with increasing labeling in area CA2/CA3 neurons, and greatest labeling in dentate gyrus (DG) granule cell somata and dendrites in mouse and rat hippocampus.
source: Similar to previous observations, in low magnification images of mouse and rat hippocampus, we observed Cav1.2 immunolabeling concentrated in CA1 neuron somata, with increasing labeling in area CA2/CA3 neurons, and greatest labeling in dentate gyrus (DG) granule cell somata and dendrites (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2A-E showing brain section immunolabeling.

claim: Kv2.1 clusters tend to colocalize with Cav1.2 clusters in DG granule cell bodies in rat hippocampus.
source: In higher magnification confocal images of DG granule cell bodies in rat hippocampus, we found that Kv2.1 clusters tended to colocalize with Cav1.2 clusters (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2F showing high-magnification imaging.

claim: The somata of rat CA1 pyramidal neurons exhibit spatial association of Cav1.2, Kv2.1, and RyR immunolabeling comparable to that seen in CHNs.
source: The somata of rat CA1 pyramidal neurons exhibited a spatial association of Cav1.2, Kv2.1, and RyR immunolabeling that was qualitatively comparable to that seen in CHNs (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2G showing brain section immunolabeling.

claim: Kv2.2 colocalizes with Cav1.2 immunolabeling in rat CA1 pyramidal cells and DG granule cells.
source: Kv2.2, which also clusters at EPJs through the same mechanism as Kv2.1 (Kirmiz et al., 2018b), similarly colocalized with Cav1.2 immunolabeling in rat CA1 pyramidal cells and DG granule cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B, with citation to Kirmiz et al., 2018b.

claim: VAP isoforms VAPA and VAPB are enriched in Kv2.1 immunopurifications from mouse brain.
source: Similar to our earlier findings, enriched in the control Kv2.1 IPs (and absent from the Kv2.1 KO brain IPs) were the VAP isoforms VAPA and VAPB (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1 showing proteomic data.

claim: RyR isoforms RyR2 and RyR3, LTCC α subunits Cav1.2 and Cav1.3, and various Cavβ auxiliary subunits are among the 50 most abundant proteins specifically present in Kv2.1 immunopurifications from mouse brain.
source: In addition, among the 50 most abundant proteins specifically present in Kv2.1 IPs (i.e., from WT and not Kv2.1 KO brain samples) were numerous proteins involved in Ca2+ signaling and/or previously reported to localize to neuronal EPJs. These included RyR isoforms RyR2 and RyR3, the LTCC α subunits Cav1.2 and Cav1.3, various Cavβ auxiliary subunits of LTCCs, as well as other proteins involved in Ca2+ signaling and homeostasis (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1 showing proteomic data.

claim: Kv2.1 is in close spatial proximity to LTCCs and RyRs at EPJs in mouse brain neurons.
source: Taken together with our imaging analyses, these findings indicate that Kv2.1 is in close spatial proximity to LTCCs and RyRs at EPJs in mouse brain neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from imaging and proteomic data.

claim: Cav1.2 is the predominant LTCC α1 subunit in hippocampus.
source: We note that while Cav1.2 is the predominant LTCC α1 subunit in hippocampus (Hell et al., 1993; Davare et al., 2001; Moosmang et al., 2005; Lacinova et al., 2008; Sinnegger-Brauns et al., 2009), where its localization on neuronal somata overlaps with Kv2.1, it was not as highly represented in these proteomic analyses as was Cav1.3, perhaps as these analyses were performed on whole brain samples.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior studies.

claim: In the presence of Kv2.1, Cav1.2 co-assembles into significantly larger clusters that show greater colocalization with the ER than in the absence of Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells.
source: However, in the presence of Kv2.1, the organization of Cav1.2 was dramatically altered, such that Cav1.2 now co-assembled with Kv2.1 into significantly larger clusters (1.05 ± 0.67 μm2) that showed greater colocalization with the ER (as indicated by the PCC of Cav1.2-GFP and BFP-Sec61β) than in the absence of Kv2.1 (Figure 3B,D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3B,D-F showing TIRF imaging and analysis.

claim: Kv2.1-induced rearrangement of Cav1.2 is accompanied by an increased occurrence of larger Cav1.2 clusters and a reduced occurrence of smaller Cav1.2 clusters in HEK293T cells.
source: The Kv2.1-induced rearrangement of Cav1.2 was accompanied by an increased occurrence of larger Cav1.2 clusters and a reduced occurrence of smaller Cav1.2 clusters, and a nearly linear relationship between the sizes of Cav1.2 and Kv2.1 clusters (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3F showing cluster size analysis.

claim: Cell surface Cav1.2-HA co-clusters with Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells.
source: Similar to cells expressing fluorescently tagged channels, we found that cell surface Cav1.2-HA also co-clustered with Kv2.1 (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3H showing cell surface immunolabeling.

claim: Kv2.1 does not alter the steady-state partitioning of Cav1.2 between PM and intracellular pools in HEK293T cells.
source: We also determined that cell surface Cav1.2-HA immunolabeling corresponded to approximately 70% of the total Cav1.2 visible in the TIRF field regardless of Kv2.1 coexpression (Figure 3I), suggesting that Kv2.1 did not alter the steady-state partitioning of Cav1.2 between PM and intracellular pools.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3I showing quantification of surface vs. total Cav1.2.

claim: Cell surface Cav1.2-HA cluster size is larger in the presence of Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells.
source: Importantly, similar to results obtained evaluating total Cav1.2, cell surface Cav1.2-HA cluster size was also larger in the presence of Kv2.1, indicating recruitment of cell surface Cav1.2 into larger clusters induced by Kv2.1 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3I showing cluster size analysis.

claim: Coexpression with Kv1.5 does not impact the clustering of cell surface Cav1.2 channels as does coexpression with Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells.
source: We also found that coexpression with the related but distinct Kv1.5 channel did not impact the clustering of cell surface Cav1.2 channels as did coexpression with Kv2.1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing immunolabeling.

claim: Cells coexpressing Kv2.1 have higher CV values for cell surface Cav1.2 than cells coexpressing Kv1.5.
source: We found that cells coexpressing Kv2.1 had higher CV values for cell surface Cav1.2 than did cells coexpressing Kv1.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1D showing CV analysis.

claim: Cell surface Kv2.1 labeling exhibits greater colocalization with cell surface Cav1.2 than does cell surface labeling for Kv1.5.
source: Cell surface Kv2.1 labeling also exhibited greater colocalization with cell surface Cav1.2 than did cell surface labeling for Kv1.5 (as indicated by PCC values, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1E showing PCC analysis.

claim: The impact of Kv2.1 expression on Cav1.2 clustering does not require Kv2.1 K+ conductance.
source: We next established that the impact of Kv2.1 expression on Cav1.2 clustering did not require Kv2.1 K+ conductance, as coexpression of a K+-impermeable point mutant (Kv2.1P404W) (Lee et al., 2003; Kirmiz et al., 2018b) induced clustering of Cav1.2 comparable to WT Kv2.1 (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3J-K showing imaging and analysis, with citations to Lee et al., 2003 and Kirmiz et al., 2018b.

claim: Coexpression with a Kv2.1 point mutant deficient in clustering (Kv2.1S586A) has no effect on Cav1.2 clustering.
source: Conversely, coexpression with a Kv2.1 point mutant (Kv2.1S586A), deficient in clustering (Lim et al., 2000) and in inducing EPJ formation (Kirmiz et al., 2018a; Kirmiz et al., 2018b), had no effect on Cav1.2 clustering (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3J-K, with citations to Lim et al., 2000; Kirmiz et al., 2018a; Kirmiz et al., 2018b.

claim: Kv2.2 channels recruit Cav1.2 into large clusters in HEK293T cells.
source: We also found that Kv2.2 channels similarly recruited Cav1.2 into large clusters (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3L showing TIRF imaging.

claim: The localization of GFP-tagged Cav1.3 is altered upon coexpression with Kv2.1 or Kv2.2 in HEK293T cells.
source: We also determined that the localization of GFP-tagged Cav1.3 was similarly altered upon coexpression with Kv2.1 or Kv2.2, implying a common mechanism for co-clustering of these two neuronal LTCCs with Kv2 channels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C showing imaging.

claim: Kv2.1 coexpression does not alter the PM localization of the T-type Ca2+ channel Cav3.1.
source: In contrast, Kv2.1 coexpression did not alter the PM localization of the T-type Ca2+ channel Cav3.1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2D-F showing imaging and analysis.

claim: The Kv2.1-mediated spatial reorganization of LTCCs is specific and related to their association with Kv2.1.
source: This observation suggests that the Kv2.1-mediated spatial reorganization of LTCCs is specific and related to their association with Kv2.1 suggested by our Kv2.1 IP experiments, a notion also supported by the absence of T-type Ca2+ channels in these IP experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Clustered but not non-clustered Kv2 channels enhance LTCC clustering and increase their localization to EPJs as a nonconducting function.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that clustered but not non-clustered Kv2 channels enhance LTCC clustering and increase their localization to EPJs as a nonconducting function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: GCaMP3-Kv2.1 and GCaMP3-Kv2.1P404W are comparably expressed in surface-localized clusters in HEK293T cells.
source: When expressed in HEK293T cells, GCaMP3-Kv2.1WT and GCaMP3-Kv2.1P404W were comparably expressed in surface-localized clusters as reported by both GxTX-633 labeling and GCaMP3 fluorescence (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing imaging and quantification.

claim: GCaMP3-Kv2.1 reports global Ca2+ spikes in rat CHNs.
source: In rat CHNs, GCaMP3-Kv2.1 exhibited clustered localization similar to other fluorescently tagged Kv2.1 isoforms (Figure 4A) and reported global Ca2+ spikes, as indicated by the synchronized increase in fluorescence across the PM at sites where the construct was clustered and also in regions with diffuse GCaMP3-Kv2.1 expression (Figure 4B, Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4A-B and Video 1 showing imaging.

claim: Rapid and stochastic Ca2+ signals occur at a subset of individual GCaMP3-Kv2.1 clusters within the soma of rat CHNs.
source: In addition to synchronized Ca2+ spikes, we also observed rapid and stochastic Ca2+ signals occurring at a subset of individual GCaMP3-Kv2.1 clusters within the soma (Figure 4B–C, Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4B-C and Video 1 showing imaging.

claim: Ca2+ signals detected by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 are confined to individual clusters such that the fluorescence of adjacent clusters remains stable.
source: These Ca2+ signals were confined to individual clusters such that the fluorescence of adjacent GCaMP3-Kv2.1 clusters < 1 µm from the active clusters remained stable (Figure 4B, compare regions of interest 2 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4B showing fluorescence traces.

claim: Ca2+ signal amplitude, frequency, and width detected by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 are insensitive to the K+ conductance of the reporter.
source: We found that Ca2+ signal amplitude, frequency, and width were insensitive to the K+ conductance of the GCaMP3-Kv2.1 reporter, as Ca2+ signals detected by a K+-impermeable variant of this construct (GCaMP3-Kv2.1P404W) showed no difference in any of these parameters relative to GCaMP3-Kv2.1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4D showing quantification.

claim: Spontaneous action potentials are associated with Ca2+ spikes reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 in rat CHNs.
source: Spontaneous action potentials were associated with Ca2+ spikes, suggesting that these synchronized, large-amplitude Ca2+ transients reflected Ca2+ entry through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels as well as Ca2+ release through RyRs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4E showing simultaneous imaging and electrophysiology.

claim: Localized Ca2+ signals reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 display no clear relationship with action potentials or other spontaneous Vm fluctuations.
source: However, unlike global Ca2+ spikes, the localized Ca2+ signals displayed no clear relationship with action potentials or other spontaneous Vm fluctuations, similar to previous observations of localized Ca2+ release events in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Berrout and Isokawa, 2009; Manita and Ross, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Berrout and Isokawa, 2009 and Manita and Ross, 2009.

claim: Localized Ca2+ signals reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 can persist in the presence of TTX.
source: We also found that the localized Ca2+ signals could persist in the presence of TTX (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), and that in some neurons, spark frequency appeared to be elevated immediately following a global Ca2+ spike (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C showing imaging data.

claim: Localized Ca2+ signals arise independently of large, uniform fluctuations in the Vm such as those that occur with action potentials.
source: Together, these observations suggest that the localized Ca2+ signals arose independently of large, uniform fluctuations in the Vm such as those that occur with action potentials.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Spontaneous, localized Ca2+ release events occur in the somata of non-transfected CHNs loaded with Cal-590 AM.
source: Using this approach, it was possible to detect spontaneous, localized Ca2+ release events in the soma that were qualitatively similar to those recorded with GCaMP3-Kv2.1 (Figure 4F–G, Video 2), although with faster kinetics in fluorescence intensity changes relative to GCaMP3-Kv2.1, likely reflecting differences in the Ca2+ binding properties of these probes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4F-G and Video 2 showing imaging.

claim: Localized Ca2+ signals in CHNs loaded with Cal-590 AM occur primarily within the soma at sites of colocalized Kv2.1 and RyR clusters.
source: Post-hoc immunolabeling of these CHNs for Kv2.1, RyRs, and the neuron-specific cytoskeletal protein MAP2 indicated that the observed localized Ca2+ signals occurred primarily within the soma at sites of colocalized Kv2.1 and RyR clusters (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4F showing post-hoc immunolabeling.

claim: Caffeine enhances the frequency of localized Ca2+ signals reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 in CHNs.
source: We found that caffeine, which sensitizes RyRs to cytosolic Ca2+, enhanced the frequency of localized Ca2+ signals (Figure 5A,B, Video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5A-B and Video 3 showing imaging data.

claim: Depletion of ER Ca2+ stores with thapsigargin eliminates local Ca2+ signals reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 in CHNs.
source: In contrast, depletion of ER Ca2+ stores with the sarco-/endo-plasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA) inhibitor thapsigargin led to an elimination of local Ca2+ signals (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5A-B showing imaging data.

claim: The LTCC agonist Bay K8644 increases Ca2+ spark frequency reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 in CHNs.
source: The frequency of these Ca2+ sparks was enhanced by activation of LTCCs with Bay K8644 (Figure 5A,B,D, Videos 4 and 5), while they were rapidly inhibited by blockade of LTCCs with nimodipine (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5A-B,D and Videos 4-5 showing imaging data.

claim: The LTCC inhibitor nimodipine rapidly inhibits Ca2+ sparks reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 in CHNs.
source: The frequency of these Ca2+ sparks was enhanced by activation of LTCCs with Bay K8644 (Figure 5A,B,D, Videos 4 and 5), while they were rapidly inhibited by blockade of LTCCs with nimodipine (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5A-B showing imaging data.

claim: The subset of GCaMP3-Kv2.1 clusters that colocalize with RyRs correspond to the clusters that produce localized Ca2+ signals.
source: Using this approach, we determined that the subset of GCaMP3-Kv2.1 clusters that colocalized with RyRs corresponded to the clusters that produced localized Ca2+ signals, either spontaneously or in response to the pharmacological modulators caffeine (Figure 5C) and Bay K8644 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5C-D showing post-hoc immunolabeling.

claim: Neuronal Ca2+ spark frequency but not amplitude correlates with RyR cluster size.
source: Similar to previous observations in vascular smooth muscle (Pritchard et al., 2018) and cardiac muscle cells (Galice et al., 2018), we found that neuronal Ca2+ spark frequency but not amplitude correlated with RyR cluster size, and that application of the LTCC agonist Bay K8644 steepened this relationship (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5E showing correlation analysis, with citations to Pritchard et al., 2018 and Galice et al., 2018.

claim: Application of Bay K8644 steepens the relationship between Ca2+ spark frequency and RyR cluster size.
source: Similar to previous observations in vascular smooth muscle (Pritchard et al., 2018) and cardiac muscle cells (Galice et al., 2018), we found that neuronal Ca2+ spark frequency but not amplitude correlated with RyR cluster size, and that application of the LTCC agonist Bay K8644 steepened this relationship (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5E showing correlation analysis.

claim: Kv2.1-associated EPJs are sites of spontaneous CICR events mediated by LTCCs and RyRs.
source: Taken together, these observations demonstrate that Kv2.1-associated EPJs are sites of spontaneous CICR events mediated by LTCCs and RyRs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyR2 can spatially associate in HEK293T cells in the presence of auxiliary subunits.
source: We found that in the presence of these auxiliary subunits, Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyR2 could spatially associate in HEK293T cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6A showing TIRF imaging.

claim: Spontaneous Ca2+ release events occur in HEK293T cells expressing Cav1.2, RyR2, and auxiliary subunits.
source: Although it was not possible to establish whether a cell expressed all transfected constructs, we observed spontaneous Ca2+ release events in a subset of cells (Figure 6B,E) that were not seen in untransfected HEK293T cells and focused our analysis on cells that exhibited this phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6B,E showing TIRF imaging.

claim: Spontaneous Ca2+ release events in HEK293T cells expressing Cav1.2, RyR2, and auxiliary subunits are rapidly blocked by the RyR inhibitor tetracaine.
source: These spontaneous Ca2+ release events were rapidly blocked by the RyR inhibitor tetracaine (Figure 6G, Video 6), suggesting that they reflected CICR mediated by RyRs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6G and Video 6 showing imaging data.

claim: Expressing Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells results in enhanced spark frequency and amplitude.
source: Expressing Kv2.1 in these cells resulted in enhanced spark frequency and amplitude (Figure 6C–D,F,J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6C-D,F,J showing imaging and quantification.

claim: Expression of Kv2.1 channels capable of clustered EPJ formation (Kv2.1WT and Kv2.1P404W) increases spark frequency in HEK293T cells.
source: Expression of Kv2.1 channels capable of clustered EPJ formation (i.e., Kv2.1WT and Kv2.1P404W) increased spark frequency, whereas non-clustering Kv2.1S586A did not (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6J showing quantification.

claim: Non-clustering Kv2.1S586A does not increase spark frequency in HEK293T cells.
source: Expression of Kv2.1 channels capable of clustered EPJ formation (i.e., Kv2.1WT and Kv2.1P404W) increased spark frequency, whereas non-clustering Kv2.1S586A did not (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6J showing quantification.

claim: Spark amplitude is enhanced by K+-conducting Kv2.1WT but not Kv2.1P404W in HEK293T cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that spark amplitude was enhanced by K+-conducting Kv2.1WT but not Kv2.1P404W (Figure 6J), suggesting that while Kv2.1-mediated clustering alone was sufficient to impact spark frequency, K+ conductance was required to impact the amplitude of reconstituted Ca2+ sparks in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6J showing quantification.

claim: Kv2.1-mediated clustering promotes the functional coupling of Cav1.2 and RyRs.
source: In conclusion, these observations indicate that Kv2.1-mediated clustering promotes the functional coupling of Cav1.2 and RyRs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Expression of Cav1.2 with Kv2.1P404W enhances peak ICa compared to cells expressing Cav1.2 alone in HEK293T cells.
source: Consistent with an influence of Cav1.2 spatial organization on its activity, we found that expression of Cav1.2 with Kv2.1P404W enhanced peak ICa as compared to cells expressing Cav1.2 alone (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7A-B showing electrophysiology data.

claim: Currents produced by Cav1.2 activate at more negative voltages in the presence of Kv2.1P404W than those produced by Cav1.2 alone in HEK293T cells.
source: Analysis of the conductance-voltage (G-V) relationship also showed an influence of Kv2.1 on the Vm threshold for Cav1.2 opening, with currents produced by Cav1.2 activating at more negative voltages in the presence of Kv2.1P404W than those produced by Cav1.2 alone, with no effect on steady-state inactivation (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7C showing G-V analysis.

claim: There is a greater reduction in the fraction of peak current remaining after 250 ms of depolarization (r250) in cells coexpressing Cav1.2 and Kv2.1P404W, suggesting elevated Ca2+-dependent inactivation (CDI).
source: However, we did observe a greater reduction in the fraction of peak current remaining after 250 ms of depolarization (r250), (Figure 7D), suggesting elevated Ca2+-dependent inactivation (CDI) of Cav1.2 in the presence of Kv2.1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7D showing r250 analysis.

claim: Cells coexpressing STAC1 with Cav1.2 and Kv2.1P404W exhibit an increase in whole-cell ICa and a hyperpolarized shift in Cav1.2 opening.
source: Cells coexpressing STAC1 with Cav1.2 and Kv2.1P404W also exhibited an increase in whole-cell ICa and a hyperpolarized shift in Cav1.2 opening, similar to results obtained without STAC1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C showing electrophysiology data.

claim: In the presence of STAC1, Cav1.2 r250 values are comparable between control cells and cells expressing Kv2.1.
source: However, in the presence of STAC1, which substantially reduces CDI in Cav1.2 (Campiglio et al., 2018), Cav1.2 r250 values were comparable between control cells and cells expressing Kv2.1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1D showing r250 analysis, with citation to Campiglio et al., 2018.

claim: Kv2.1P404W enhances Cav1.2-mediated Ca2+ influx measured by Rhod-2 fluorescence in HEK293T cells.
source: Measurement of Ca2+-induced fluorescence increases in cells loaded with the Ca2+-sensitive dye Rhod-2 via the patch pipette also revealed an enhancing effect of Kv2.1P404W on Cav1.2-mediated Ca2+ influx (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7E showing fluorescence measurements.

claim: HEK293T cells expressing Cav1.2 and either Kv2.1WT or Kv2.1P404W display greater K+-depolarization induced Ca2+ influx than control cells.
source: Similarly, HEK293T cells loaded with the Ca2+ dye Fluo-4 and expressing Cav1.2 and either Kv2.1WT or Kv2.1P404W displayed greater K+-depolarization induced Ca2+ influx than control cells (Figure 7F–G), further supporting that K+-conducting as well as -nonconducting isoforms of Kv2.1 augment Cav1.2 activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7F-G showing fluorescence measurements.

claim: Nitrendipine-sensitive Qon values produced by Cav1.2 alone are comparable to those measured in the presence of Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells.
source: Nitrendipine-sensitive Qon values produced by Cav1.2 alone were comparable to those measured in the presence of Kv2.1, indicating that the increased ICa in cells coexpressing Kv2.1 was not associated with an increase in the number of PM Cav1.2 channels (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7I showing gating current analysis.

claim: The nitrendipine-sensitive Itail is significantly greater in the presence of Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells.
source: However, the nitrendipine-sensitive Itail was significantly greater in the presence of Kv2.1, demonstrating that the open probability and/or conductance of Cav1.2 was increased when coexpressed with Kv2.1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7I showing tail current analysis.

claim: The Kv2.1-dependent increase in ICa apparently comes from enhanced Cav1.2 voltage sensor coupling to channel opening.
source: As comparable Qon values (i.e., Cav1.2 voltage sensor movement) produced a larger Itail in the presence of Kv2.1, these data taken together with the altered G-V curve shown in Figure 7C suggest that the Kv2.1-dependent increase in ICa apparently came from enhanced Cav1.2 voltage sensor coupling to channel opening.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the electrophysiology data.

claim: Cells coexpressing Cav1.2 and DsRed-Kv2.1P404W display significantly more sparklets than control cells expressing Cav1.2 alone at a holding potential of −70 mV.
source: In contrast, control cells coexpressing Cav1.2 and DsRed-Kv2.1P404W displayed significantly more sparklets than control cells expressing Cav1.2 alone and a higher level of basal activity as measured by nPs, where n is the number of quantal levels of Cav1.2 opening and Ps is the probability of sparklet occurrence (Figure 8C–E,I,J,L, Video 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 8C-E,I,J,L and Video 8 showing sparklet imaging and analysis.

claim: DsRed-Kv2.1P404W coexpression results in near-maximal activation of Cav1.2-mediated sparklets at −70 mV holding potential.
source: Interestingly, Bay K8644 treatment did not result in any further enhancement in nPs in cells expressing DsRed-Kv2.1P404W (Figure 8J), suggesting that DsRed-Kv2.1P404W coexpression may result in near-maximal activation of Cav1.2-mediated sparklets at this hyperpolarized membrane potential.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 8J showing sparklet analysis.

claim: The nearest-neighbor distance (NND) of individual sparklet sites is significantly reduced in the presence of Kv2.1.
source: Many sparklets occurred near clusters of Kv2.1 channels, and we found that the nearest-neighbor distance (NND) of individual sparklet sites was significantly reduced in the presence of Kv2.1 (Figure 8K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 8K showing NND analysis.

claim: Kv2.1 enhances the open probability of Cav1.2 channels and increases the proximity of spontaneously active Cav1.2 channels to each other.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that Kv2.1 enhanced the open probability of Cav1.2 channels and increased the proximity of spontaneously active Cav1.2 channels to each other.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the sparklet data.

claim: Whole-cell Ba2+ currents (IBa) at +10 mV are larger in CHNs from WT mice than those measured in Kv2.1 KO CHNs.
source: Similar to the impact of Kv2.1 on LTCCs in HEK293T cells, whole-cell Ba2+ currents (IBa) at +10 mV (Figure 9A), as well as LTCC tail currents (Figure 9B,C) were larger in CHNs from WT mice than those measured in Kv2.1 KO CHNs (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 9A-C showing electrophysiology data.

claim: The reduced IBa observed in Kv2.1 KO CHNs is primarily due to a reduction in the nimodipine-sensitive component of the current.
source: To isolate the LTCC component of IBa, we applied the LTCC gating inhibitor nimodipine (10 µM), and found that the reduced IBa observed in Kv2.1 KO CHNs (Figure 9A–C) was primarily due to a reduction in the nimodipine-sensitive component of the current (Figure 9A,B,E), with no apparent difference in the nimodipine-resistant current (Figure 9A,B,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 9A-E showing electrophysiology data.

claim: Nimodipine-sensitive Qon is not significantly different between control and Kv2.1 KO CHNs.
source: We also examined nimodipine-sensitive gating and ionic tail currents when the Vm was stepped to the IBa reversal potential and found that while Qon was not significantly different between control and Kv2.1 KO CHNs, peak Itail was reduced in Kv2.1 KO CHNs (Figure 9F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 9F-G showing gating current analysis.

claim: Peak Itail is reduced in Kv2.1 KO CHNs compared to control CHNs.
source: We also examined nimodipine-sensitive gating and ionic tail currents when the Vm was stepped to the IBa reversal potential and found that while Qon was not significantly different between control and Kv2.1 KO CHNs, peak Itail was reduced in Kv2.1 KO CHNs (Figure 9F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 9F-G showing tail current analysis.

claim: Kv2.1 enhances neuronal LTCC activity through enhanced coupling efficiency between LTCC voltage-sensor movement and channel opening due to Kv2.1-mediated clustering.
source: The data in Figures 7 and 8 (from exogenously expressed channels in HEK293T cells) and Figure 9 (from endogenously expressed channels in CHNs) show that Kv2.1 enhances neuronal LTCC activity and suggest that the underlying mechanism in both experimental systems involves enhanced coupling efficiency between LTCC voltage-sensor movement and channel opening due to Kv2.1-mediated clustering.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the electrophysiology data.

claim: Cav1.2 labeling is increased in pyramidal neurons in area CA1 in Kv2.1 KO brain sections, both within the cell bodies and in the apical dendrites.
source: However, Cav1.2 labeling was increased in pyramidal neurons in area CA1 in Kv2.1 KO brain sections, both within the cell bodies and in the apical dendrites (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 10C showing immunolabeling quantification.

claim: In adult mice lacking functional Kv2.1 channels, Cav1.2 expression may be elevated, potentially as a compensatory mechanism to overcome reduced Cav1.2 channel function.
source: These results suggest that in adult mice lacking functional Kv2.1 channels, Cav1.2 expression may be elevated, potentially as a compensatory mechanism to overcome reduced Cav1.2 channel function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the immunolabeling data.

claim: Kv2.1 KO CHNs have reduced colocalization between Cav1.2 clusters and RyR compared to WT CHNs.
source: We found that compared to WT CHNs, Kv2.1 KO CHNs had reduced colocalization between Cav1.2 clusters and RyR, decreased size of RyR clusters, and increased distance between Cav1.2 clusters (Figure 11C–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 11C-F showing morphological analysis.

claim: Kv2.1 KO CHNs have decreased size of RyR clusters compared to WT CHNs.
source: We found that compared to WT CHNs, Kv2.1 KO CHNs had reduced colocalization between Cav1.2 clusters and RyR, decreased size of RyR clusters, and increased distance between Cav1.2 clusters (Figure 11C–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 11C-F showing morphological analysis.

claim: Kv2.1 KO CHNs have increased distance between Cav1.2 clusters compared to WT CHNs.
source: We found that compared to WT CHNs, Kv2.1 KO CHNs had reduced colocalization between Cav1.2 clusters and RyR, decreased size of RyR clusters, and increased distance between Cav1.2 clusters (Figure 11C–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 11C-F showing morphological analysis.

claim: The number of Cav1.2 clusters per µm2 of somatic membrane does not differ between WT and Kv2.1 KO CHNs.
source: However, unlike the increased Cav1.2 immunolabeling found in adult Kv2.1 KO mouse brain sections, we found that the number of Cav1.2 clusters per µm2 of somatic membrane did not differ between WT and Kv2.1 KO CHNs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The presence of Kv2.1 promotes the spatial coupling of Cav1.2 to RyRs in CHNs.
source: These observations suggests that while compensatory changes in Cav1.2 expression did not occur in cultured Kv2.1 KO CHNs after approximately two weeks in vitro as it did in adult brain neurons in vivo, the presence of Kv2.1 promoted the spatial coupling of Cav1.2 to RyRs, consistent with our results in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Spontaneous sparks in WT mouse CHNs are associated with Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyR clusters identified by post-hoc immunolabeling.
source: Similar to rat CHNs, we observed spontaneous sparks in WT mouse CHNs that were associated with Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyR clusters identified by post-hoc immunolabeling (Figure 11G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 11G showing imaging and immunolabeling.

claim: Loss of Kv2.1 is associated with a significant reduction in spark frequency relative to WT control CHNs.
source: Consistent with the reduced colocalization of Cav1.2 and RyRs in Kv2.1 KO CHNs, we found that loss of Kv2.1 was associated with a significant reduction in spark frequency relative to WT control CHNs (Figure 11H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 11H showing spark frequency analysis.

claim: Kv2.1 channels promote the spatial and functional association of endogenous Cav1.2 and RyRs in neurons.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that Kv2.1 channels promote the spatial and functional association of endogenous Cav1.2 and RyRs in neurons, as well as the corresponding exogenous channels in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: A nonconducting function of PM Kv2.1 channels is to anchor the ER to the PM via a direct interaction with ER VAP proteins.
source: We propose that a nonconducting function of PM Kv2.1 channels is to not only anchor the ER to the PM via a direct interaction with ER VAP proteins (Johnson et al., 2018; Kirmiz et al., 2018a), but also to promote the organization of Cav1.2 channels into clusters in direct apposition to nearby ER-localized RyRs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Johnson et al., 2018 and Kirmiz et al., 2018a.

claim: Kv2.1 promotes the organization of Cav1.2 channels into clusters in direct apposition to nearby ER-localized RyRs.
source: We propose that a nonconducting function of PM Kv2.1 channels is to not only anchor the ER to the PM via a direct interaction with ER VAP proteins (Johnson et al., 2018; Kirmiz et al., 2018a), but also to promote the organization of Cav1.2 channels into clusters in direct apposition to nearby ER-localized RyRs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed model based on the data.

claim: Kv2.1-mediated clustering increases the activity of Cav1.2.
source: Our data indicate that Kv2.1-mediated clustering also increases the activity of Cav1.2.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Enhanced spontaneous openings of Cav1.2 channels at negative potentials allow a small amount of Ca2+ to enter the cell at EPJs, activating nearby RyRs by CICR.
source: The enhanced spontaneous openings of Cav1.2 channels at negative potentials is evidenced by the increased frequency of sparklets, which allow a small amount of Ca2+ to enter the cell at EPJs, activating nearby RyRs by the mechanism of CICR.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Ca2+ sparks at Kv2.1-associated EPJs occur independently of action potentials.
source: The resulting Ca2+ sparks occur independently of action potentials.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Colocalization of LTCCs with Kv2.1 is dynamically regulated and sensitive to neuronal activity.
source: The Kv2.1-mediated association of Cav1.2 with EPJs appears to be dynamically regulated and sensitive to neuronal activity, as acute dispersal of Kv2.1 clusters in CHNs by glutamate stimulation reduced Cav1.2 association with RyRs, whereas suppression of neuronal activity with TTX (which increases Kv2.1 phosphorylation and clustering) enhanced spatial coupling of Cav1.2 and RyRs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: LTCCs are recruited to Kv2.1-associated EPJs.
source: Together, these findings indicate that LTCCs are recruited to Kv2.1-associated EPJs, a property we found was not shared by the T-type Ca2+ channel Cav3.1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: The proteins mediating Cav1.2 clustering in dendritic spines and at somatic EPJs may be distinct.
source: The absence of these known LTCC clustering proteins from our proteomic analyses of proteins in close spatial proximity to Kv2.1, and our observation that expression of Kv2.1 increases Cav1.2 clustering in heterologous HEK293T cells, suggests that the proteins mediating Cav1.2 clustering in dendritic spines and at somatic EPJs may be distinct.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data.

claim: Kv2.1 clustering and induction of EPJs is necessary for its spatial association with LTCCs.
source: These findings support that Kv2.1 clustering and induction of EPJs is necessary for its spatial association with LTCCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Tethering of LTCCs at or near Kv2-associated EPJs could be mediated by an intermediary recruited to Kv2.1-mediated EPJs.
source: This is consistent with a model whereby tethering of LTCCs at or near Kv2-associated EPJs could be mediated by an intermediary recruited to Kv2.1-mediated EPJs, perhaps even one of the proteins identified in our proteomics analyses (although note a different study did not observe this effect of junctophilin-2 coexpression [Dixon et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation about the mechanism, with citation to Dixon et al., 2015.

claim: It is unlikely that RyRs are directly recruited to EPJs by Kv2 channels.
source: It is unlikely that RyRs are directly recruited to EPJs by Kv2 channels, as RyR clusters persist in CHNs exposed to treatments that disperse Kv2.1 clusters (Misonou et al., 2005a) and while reduced in size in CA1 pyramidal neurons in the double Kv2.1/Kv2.2 knockout (Kirmiz et al., 2018a), in general RyR clusters persist in neurons in the brains of mice lacking Kv2 channels (Mandikian et al., 2014; Kirmiz et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior studies.

claim: LTCC activity is sensitive to its spatial organization in the PM, influenced by its proximity to adjacent LTCCs and its localization to specific neuronal compartments.
source: Thus, LTCC activity is sensitive to its spatial organization in the PM, influenced by its proximity to adjacent LTCCs (Navedo et al., 2005; Navedo et al., 2010; Dixon et al., 2012; Moreno et al., 2016) and also to its localization to specific neuronal compartments (Hall et al., 2013; Tseng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior studies.

claim: The subcellular localization and activity of somatic Cav1.2 channels are influenced by Kv2.1, which increases both Cav1.2 clustering and its opening at polarized Vm values.
source: Here, we show that the subcellular localization and activity of somatic Cav1.2 channels are influenced by Kv2.1, which increases both Cav1.2 clustering and its opening at polarized Vm values.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: The reduced whole-cell LTCC currents and impaired association of somatic Cav1.2 with RyRs in Kv2.1 KO CHNs suggests that Kv2.1 serves a dual targeting/modulation function for LTCCs within the soma and proximal dendrites.
source: The reduced whole-cell LTCC currents and impaired association of somatic Cav1.2 with RyRs in Kv2.1 KO CHNs suggests that Kv2.1 serves this dual targeting/modulation function for LTCCs within the soma and proximal dendrites.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data.

claim: Coexpression of Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells increases whole-cell Cav1.2 current amplitude without an apparent change in the number of Cav1.2 channels present on the PM.
source: In both CHNs and HEK293T cells, currents resulting from the opening of endogenous and exogenous Cav1.2 channels, respectively, are increased in the presence of Kv2.1. In HEK293T cells, Cav1.2 channels coexpressed with clustered Kv2.1 are activated at more polarized Vm values relative to those produced by Cav1.2 alone. Moreover, coexpression of Cav1.2 with nonconducting Kv2.1 increases the frequency of spontaneous Cav1.2 channel openings in HEK293T cells as reflected in an increased frequency of Ca2+ sparklets. The Kv2.1-dependent increase in whole-cell Cav1.2 current amplitude in both HEK293T cells and CHNs occurs without an apparent change in the number of Cav1.2 channels present on the PM, as total Cav1.2 on-gating charges were unaltered by coexpression with Kv2.1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the data.

claim: Coupling of Cav1.2 voltage sensor movement to channel opening is enhanced in the presence of Kv2.1.
source: Instead, it appears that coupling of Cav1.2 voltage sensor movement to channel opening is enhanced in the presence of Kv2.1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the data.

claim: One possible mechanism for the Kv2.1-dependent increase in ICa is that Kv2.1-induced clustering at EPJs increases the probability of physical interactions between Cav1.2 channels, which promotes their cooperative gating.
source: First, the increase in ICa and leftward shift in the voltage-dependence of activation that we observed upon coexpression of Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells are similar to those observed during optogenetic induction of Cav1.2 channel oligomerization (Navedo et al., 2010; Dixon et al., 2012). Thus, one possible mechanism is that Kv2.1-induced clustering at EPJs increases the probability of physical interactions between Cav1.2 channels, which promotes their cooperative gating.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation about the mechanism, with citations to Navedo et al., 2010 and Dixon et al., 2012.

claim: A second possibility is that Kv2.1 functions as an auxiliary voltage sensor for Cav1.2 channels, perhaps through a direct intermolecular interaction of the two channels.
source: A second possibility is that Kv2.1 functions as an auxiliary voltage sensor for Cav1.2 channels, perhaps through a direct intermolecular interaction of the two channels.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation about the mechanism.

claim: A third potential explanation for the Kv2.1-mediated increase in Cav1.2 channel activity is that Cav1.2 is modulated by signaling molecules that it encounters when recruited to EPJs by Kv2.1.
source: A third potential explanation for the Kv2.1-mediated increase in Cav1.2 channel activity is that Cav1.2 is modulated by signaling molecules that it encounters when recruited to EPJs by Kv2.1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Ca2+ spark frequency increased when neurons were exposed to Cav1.2 channel agonists and decreased by blockade of LTCCs.
source: Accordingly, Ca2+ spark frequency increased when neurons were exposed to Cav1.2 channel agonists and decreased by blockade of LTCCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the data.

claim: Loss of Kv2.1 expression is associated with a decrease in Ca2+ spark frequency, likely because of decreased spatial association of Cav1.2 and RyRs, decreased RyR cluster size, and decreased LTCC currents.
source: Loss of Kv2.1 expression was also associated with a decrease in Ca2+ spark frequency, likely because of decreased spatial association of Cav1.2 and RyRs, decreased RyR cluster size, and decreased LTCC currents.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the data.

claim: Only a subset of Kv2.1-associated EPJs possess the molecular machinery required to generate localized Ca2+ signals.
source: As Kv2.1 clusters intrinsically represent EPJs by nature of their formation via an interaction with ER-resident VAPs (Johnson et al., 2018; Kirmiz et al., 2018a; Kirmiz et al., 2018b), our observation that localized Ca2+ signals occurred only at a subset of GCaMP3-Kv2.1 clusters suggests that only a subset of Kv2.1-associated EPJs possess the molecular machinery required to generate these Ca2+ signals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data, with citations to Johnson et al., 2018; Kirmiz et al., 2018a; Kirmiz et al., 2018b.

claim: Kv2.1-mediated somatodendritic EPJs provide a molecular platform to elevate local Ca2+ at individual EPJs without an increase in global Ca2+.
source: Our findings indicate that Kv2.1-mediated somatodendritic EPJs provide a molecular platform to elevate local Ca2+ at individual EPJs without an increase in global Ca2+, but that can also contribute to global, action potential-induced increases in cytoplasmic Ca2+.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Sparks can occur independently in neighboring Kv2.1-containing EPJs, suggesting a mechanism for compartmentalized Ca2+ signaling in the aspiny regions of neurons.
source: That sparks can occur independently in neighboring Kv2.1-containing EPJs suggests a mechanism for compartmentalized Ca2+ signaling in the aspiny regions of neurons (somata, proximal dendrites, axon initial segment) in which Kv2.1 clusters are located.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data.

claim: Somatic LTCC- and RyR-mediated Ca2+ release activates KCa3.1 channels in hippocampal neurons, reducing spike frequency.
source: While this mode of BK channel activation has not been observed in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Ross, 2012), somatic LTCC- and RyR-mediated Ca2+ release has recently been demonstrated to activate KCa3.1 channels in hippocampal neurons, reducing spike frequency (Sahu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Ross, 2012 and Sahu et al., 2019.

claim: Somatodendritic LTCCs are preferentially coupled to activation of signaling pathways resulting in changes in gene expression.
source: Somatodendritic LTCCs are preferentially coupled to activation of signaling pathways resulting in changes in gene expression (Wheeler et al., 2012; Wild et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Wheeler et al., 2012 and Wild et al., 2019.

claim: Kv2.1-mediated organization and regulation of somatic LTCCs provides a molecular mechanism to control local Ca2+ influx and serve as an organizer of Ca2+ signaling microdomains.
source: The results presented here suggest that Kv2.1-mediated organization and regulation of somatic LTCCs provides a molecular mechanism to control local Ca2+ influx and serve as an organizer of Ca2+ signaling microdomains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Acute ischemic or depolarizing events lead to Ca2+-dependent dispersal of Kv2.1 clusters and hyperpolarize its Vm activation threshold, potentially as a homeostatic mechanism to reduce neuronal activity and Ca2+ overload.
source: Previous work from us (Misonou et al., 2004; Misonou et al., 2005b) and others (Mulholland et al., 2008; Aras et al., 2009) has shown that acute ischemic or depolarizing events lead to Ca2+-dependent dispersal of Kv2.1 clusters and hyperpolarize its Vm activation threshold, potentially as a homeostatic mechanism to reduce neuronal activity and Ca2+ overload that can lead to excitotoxicity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior studies.

claim: The Ca2+-dependent dispersal of Kv2.1 clusters and the resulting dissociation of Cav1.2 and RyRs may represent a negative feedback loop to limit excessive increases in cytoplasmic Ca2+.
source: In our experiments here, we determined that Kv2.1-mediated clustering was associated with enhanced functional coupling of Cav1.2 and RyRs, as well as increased activation of Cav1.2 at polarized Vm values. Therefore, the Ca2+-dependent dispersal of Kv2.1 clusters and the resulting dissociation of Cav1.2 and RyRs may represent a negative feedback loop to limit excessive increases in cytoplasmic Ca2+.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data.

claim: Activity-dependent declustering of Kv2.1 may help to reduce currents conducted by LTCCs, both through increased activation of hyperpolarizing Kv2.1 currents at polarized Vm and through limiting Cav1.2 activity by altering its spatial organization in the PM.
source: Activity-dependent declustering of Kv2.1 may also help to reduce currents conducted by LTCCs, both through increased activation of hyperpolarizing Kv2.1 currents at polarized Vm (opposing activation of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels) and also through limiting Cav1.2 activity by altering its spatial organization in the PM.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The spatial association of Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyRs is preserved in intact adult mouse and rat brains and can be recapitulated in heterologous cells.
source: Overall, the findings presented here identify a molecular structure underlying the spontaneous somatodendritic Ca2+ signals previously observed in hippocampal pyramidal neurons. While our live cell experiments were primarily confined to CHNs cultured for 9–15 days in vitro, our data indicate that the spatial association of Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyRs is preserved in intact adult mouse and rat brains and can be recapitulated in heterologous cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the data.

claim: Somatodendritic Ca2+ sparks have been observed in acute hippocampal slices obtained from rats aged P3-P80.
source: Moreover, somatodendritic Ca2+ sparks have been observed in acute hippocampal slices obtained from rats aged P3-P80 (Miyazaki et al., 2012), suggesting that these Ca2+ release events serve functional roles that emerge early in pyramidal neuron development and continue beyond this period.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Miyazaki et al., 2012.
